newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks soar to post second biggest daily gain.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks soar to post second biggest daily gain.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks posted their second-largest daily gain ever on Tuesday as investors sought safety in big-name shares, while bonds rose after a solid Treasury note auction.
The dollar firmed after an important group of German economists predicted it would rally in coming months and U.S. negotiators reportedly neared a deal on the federal budget.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 173.38 points, or 2.60 percent, at 6,833.59.

The gain for the world's most widely watched stock index was second in point terms only to the 187-point leap that took placed two days after the "Black Monday" stock market crash of Oct. 19, 1987, when the 30-stock Dow crumbled 508 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 1,533 to 955 on active volume of 501 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Despite the powerhouse performance by blue chips, analysts were wary of the mixed performance in the broader market. Indeed, buyers appeared extremely focused and largely shunned mid-sized and smaller companies.

"People are looking for companies with strong earnings and strong balance sheets," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "Money is moving towards predictability rather than projections."
Seasonal factors may have contributed to the sudden burst of buying, analysts said.

"A lot of the money we saw today is money that was put in retirement accounts by the April 15 (tax) deadline," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "And that money's going directly into index funds."
It was on April 15 that the Dow last managed a rise of this magnitude, posting a 135-point rally that then stood as the index's second best.
Again on Tuesday, there was evidence of clear investor preference for safety over speculation.
"What's very clear in the composition of mutual fund flows is that investors have become more risk averse," said Doug Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan.
"If you look at the past four weeks, 60 percent of the new money is going to income or growth and income funds," he said.
Such funds, and the stocks they invest in, offer a combination of healthy dividend yields and lower volatilty that investors crave during periods of instability, Cliggott said.
The Dow last set a record high on March 11, with a close of 7,085.16.
The 30-year Treasury bond rose 18/32, or $5.625 per $1,000 face value, lowering its yield to 7.04 percent from 7.09 percent at Monday's close. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
The dollar rallied to 1.7160 German marks late Tuesday, up from 1.6982 late Monday. It also rose to 126.32 Japanese yen from 125.34 yen.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for May delivery closed 78 cents lower at $19.60 a barrel as traders shrugged off potential supply threats from a strike in Nigeria.
May unleaded gasoline ended down 1.03 cents a gallon at 61.77 cents, and May heating oil ended down 0.65 cent a gallon at 54.83 cents.
Coffee prices fell as traders shrugged off a strike in Colombia and took profits instead.
At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for May delivery closed 3.70 cents a pound lower at 211.70 cents and down sharply from the life-of-contract high of 224.00 cents set on Monday.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed 17.4 points higher at 4,346.1. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed 7.21 points, or 0.04 percent, lower at 18,544.45.
